Congenital Heart Disease

Level: Advanced
Topic: Pediatric / Critical Care / Cardiology
Duration: 90 minutes

Arrival Scenario

You’re called to a pediatrician’s office for a 3-week-old infant. The baby has been “fussy and not eating well” for 2 days. Mom says he “turns blue sometimes” during feeds.

On exam: pale, diaphoretic, tachypneic (RR 68), grunting, weak cry. Heart rate 185. Liver edge palpable 2 cm below costal margin. Weak femoral pulses. SpO2 82% on room air.

The pediatrician hands you a referral letter: “Suspected congenital heart disease - needs pediatric cardiology eval.”

This baby is in heart failure. And you need to know why.

Warm-Up Questions

Before we break down the anatomy, answer these:

  1. What’s the difference between cyanotic and acyanotic congenital heart disease?
  2. What is a shunt? Left-to-right vs. right-to-left?
  3. What are the signs of heart failure in an infant?
  4. What is a duct-dependent lesion?
  5. Why would a baby with certain heart defects NEED to stay hypoxic?

These aren’t trivia. They’re life-or-death concepts.

Explanation / Breakdown

Congenital Heart Disease (CHD) Overview

Congenital heart disease = structural heart defect present at birth.

Incidence: ~1% of live births (most common congenital defect)

Two main categories:

  1. Acyanotic (pink baby) - usually left-to-right shunts
  2. Cyanotic (blue baby) - usually right-to-left shunts or mixing lesions

Understanding Shunts

Shunt = abnormal connection allowing blood to bypass normal circulation

Left-to-Right Shunt:

  • Blood flows from high-pressure left side → low-pressure right side
  • Result: Too much blood goes to lungs (pulmonary overcirculation)
  • Presentation: CHF symptoms, not cyanotic (until Eisenmenger syndrome develops)
  • Examples: VSD, ASD, PDA

Right-to-Left Shunt:

  • Blood flows from right side → left side, bypassing lungs
  • Result: Deoxygenated blood enters systemic circulation
  • Presentation: Cyanosis (blue baby)
  • Examples: Tetralogy of Fallot, transposition, truncus arteriosus

Acyanotic (Left-to-Right Shunt) Lesions

Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)

What it is: Hole in the wall between ventricles

Pathophysiology:

  • Left ventricle pressure > right ventricle pressure
  • Blood shunts left → right
  • Extra blood floods lungs → pulmonary overcirculation → CHF

Presentation:

  • Small VSD: Loud holosystolic murmur, asymptomatic (often closes spontaneously)
  • Large VSD: CHF symptoms (FTT, tachypnea, diaphoresis, hepatomegaly), frequent respiratory infections

Management:

  • Small: Observation
  • Large: Surgery (patch closure)
  • Acute CHF: Diuretics, afterload reduction

Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)

What it is: Hole in the wall between atria

Pathophysiology:

  • Left atrium pressure > right atrium pressure
  • Blood shunts left → right (less dramatic than VSD)
  • Pulmonary overcirculation develops over time

Presentation:

  • Often asymptomatic in childhood
  • Fixed split S2 (classic finding)
  • CHF symptoms in adulthood if uncorrected
  • Increased risk of stroke (paradoxical embolism)

Management:

  • Observation vs. surgical/catheter-based closure

Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)

What it is: Ductus arteriosus fails to close after birth

Normal physiology: Ductus connects pulmonary artery to aorta in fetus, closes within days of birth

Pathophysiology:

  • Aorta pressure > pulmonary artery pressure
  • Blood shunts aorta → PA → floods lungs
  • Increased pulmonary blood flow → CHF

Presentation:

  • Continuous “machinery” murmur (systole + diastole)
  • Bounding pulses (wide pulse pressure)
  • CHF symptoms if large

Management:

  • Indomethacin (closes duct in premature infants)
  • Surgical ligation if medical management fails

Cyanotic (Right-to-Left Shunt) Lesions

Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

What it is: Four defects occurring together

The Four Defects:

  1. VSD (large)
  2. Pulmonary stenosis (RV outflow obstruction)
  3. Overriding aorta (aorta sits over VSD)
  4. Right ventricular hypertrophy (compensatory)

Pathophysiology:

  • Pulmonary stenosis → high RV pressure
  • Blood shunts right → left through VSD
  • Deoxygenated blood enters aorta → cyanosis

Presentation:

  • Cyanosis (worse with crying, feeding, exertion)
  • Tet spells (hypercyanotic episodes)
  • Squatting after exertion (increases systemic resistance → more blood to lungs)
  • “Boot-shaped” heart on CXR

Tet Spell (Hypercyanotic Crisis):

  • Severe cyanosis, irritability, loss of consciousness
  • Triggered by crying, defecation, feeding
  • Emergency: Can lead to syncope, seizures, death

Tet Spell Management:

  • Knee-chest position (increases SVR)
  • 100% O2 (won’t help much, but give it)
  • IV fluids (increase preload)
  • Morphine (decreases SVR, calms infant)
  • Phenylephrine (increases SVR, controversial)

Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA)

What it is: Aorta and pulmonary artery are switched

Pathophysiology:

  • Aorta arises from RV (carries deoxygenated blood to body)
  • PA arises from LV (carries oxygenated blood back to lungs)
  • Two separate circuits - incompatible with life unless mixing occurs

Survival depends on:

  • Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA)
  • Atrial septal defect (ASD)
  • Ventricular septal defect (VSD)

Presentation:

  • Severe cyanosis within hours of birth
  • Worsens as ductus closes
  • Duct-dependent lesion - needs prostaglandin E1 to survive

Management:

  • Prostaglandin E1 infusion (keeps ductus open)
  • Balloon atrial septostomy (create/enlarge ASD for mixing)
  • Arterial switch operation (definitive repair)

Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome (HLHS)

What it is: Left ventricle, mitral valve, aortic valve underdeveloped/absent

Pathophysiology:

  • RV must supply both pulmonary and systemic circulation
  • Systemic blood flow depends on PDA (duct-dependent)
  • Mixing occurs at atrial level

Presentation:

  • Appears normal at birth (ductus is open)
  • Rapid deterioration as ductus closes (12-48 hours)
  • Shock, cyanosis, respiratory distress
  • Weak/absent pulses
  • Gray, mottled skin

Management:

  • Prostaglandin E1 immediately (keeps duct open - this baby will die without it)
  • IV fluids cautiously (preload management)
  • Avoid high FiO2 (causes pulmonary vasodilation → steals blood from systemic circulation)
  • Immediate transport to pediatric cardiac center
  • Norwood procedure (3-stage surgical palliation) or transplant

Truncus Arteriosus

What it is: Single arterial trunk arises from heart (instead of separate aorta + PA)

Pathophysiology:

  • Complete mixing of oxygenated + deoxygenated blood
  • Always has VSD
  • Pulmonary overcirculation (CHF) + mild cyanosis

Presentation:

  • Cyanosis + CHF symptoms
  • Loud systolic murmur
  • Bounding pulses

Management:

  • CHF management
  • Surgical repair

Duct-Dependent Lesions

Certain lesions require the ductus arteriosus to remain open for survival:

Duct-Dependent for Systemic Flow:

  • Hypoplastic left heart syndrome
  • Critical aortic stenosis
  • Interrupted aortic arch
  • Coarctation of the aorta (severe)

Duct-Dependent for Pulmonary Flow:

  • Pulmonary atresia
  • Critical pulmonary stenosis
  • Tricuspid atresia

If the duct closes → the baby dies.

Treatment: Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) keeps the ductus open

PGE1 Dosing: 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min IV infusion

Side Effects: Apnea (have intubation equipment ready), hypotension, fever

Common Mistakes

Mistake #1: Giving High-Flow O2 to All Cyanotic Babies

In duct-dependent systemic lesions (like HLHS), high O2 causes pulmonary vasodilation → more blood to lungs → less blood to body → worsens shock. Keep SpO2 75-85%.

Mistake #2: Missing the Diagnosis Because “Baby Looks Fine”

Many CHD babies compensate well initially. Then they crash suddenly when the ductus closes.

Mistake #3: Treating “Pneumonia” in a Baby with Undiagnosed CHD

CHF looks like pneumonia (tachypnea, crackles, poor feeding). Don’t assume it’s infection.

Mistake #4: Aggressive Fluid Resuscitation in CHF

These babies are in fluid overload, not dehydration. Fluids can worsen CHF.

Mistake #5: Delaying Transport for “Stabilization”

Duct-dependent lesions need PGE1 and pediatric cardiac surgery. Get moving.

Clinical Pearls

💎 Cyanosis that doesn’t improve with O2 = cardiac problem until proven otherwise.

💎 Differential cyanosis (pink upper body, blue lower body) = think coarctation or interrupted aortic arch.

💎 Reverse differential cyanosis (blue upper, pink lower) = think transposition with PDA.

💎 Absent or weak femoral pulses in a neonate = coarctation of the aorta.

💎 If a baby crashes at 2-7 days of life = think duct-dependent lesion (ductus is closing).

💎 Tet spell = knee-chest position + O2 + fluids + morphine.

💎 HLHS babies can’t tolerate high O2. Keep SpO2 75-85% (counterintuitive but critical).

💎 A loud murmur doesn’t always mean severe disease. Small VSDs are loud. Large VSDs with CHF may have soft murmurs.

💎 Diaphoresis during feeding in an infant = heart failure.

💎 If you suspect duct-dependent CHD, call for PGE1 early. Don’t wait for the crash.

Decision Trees

Cyanotic Newborn Assessment

Cyanotic Newborn
    ↓
Give 100% O2
    ↓
Cyanosis improves?
    YES → Likely respiratory cause
        - Pneumonia, TTN, RDS, meconium aspiration
        - Continue respiratory support
    NO → Likely cardiac cause (or severe lung disease)
        ↓
        Check pulses (all 4 extremities)
        ↓
        Weak/absent femoral pulses?
            YES → Coarctation, interrupted arch, HLHS
            NO → Continue assessment
        ↓
        Differential cyanosis?
            YES → Coarctation with PDA
        ↓
        Signs of CHF? (tachypnea, hepatomegaly, poor feeding)
            YES → Mixing lesion (TGA, truncus, TAPVR)
        ↓
        Suspect duct-dependent lesion?
            ↓
            Contact pediatric cardiology
            Prepare PGE1 infusion
            Intubation equipment ready
            Immediate transport to cardiac center

Duct-Dependent Lesion Management

Suspected Duct-Dependent CHD
    ↓
IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
    ↓
1. Contact pediatric cardiac center
2. Request PGE1 (if available)
3. Prepare for potential apnea (intubation equipment)
4. IV access (IO if difficult)
    ↓
Is PGE1 Available?
    YES → Start PGE1 infusion
        - Dose: 0.05-0.1 mcg/kg/min
        - Monitor for apnea
        - Intubate if apnea occurs
    NO → Supportive care during transport
        - Minimize O2 if HLHS suspected
        - IV fluids cautiously
        - Keep baby warm
        - Rapid transport
    ↓
Oxygen Management Based on Lesion:
    ↓
    Duct-dependent for SYSTEMIC flow (HLHS)?
        → Keep SpO2 75-85%
        → Avoid high O2 (worsens shock)
    ↓
    Duct-dependent for PULMONARY flow (PA, PS)?
        → Give O2 as needed
        → Higher SpO2 okay
    ↓
Transport with continuous monitoring
Anticipate deterioration

Practice Cases

Case 1: The Blue Baby

Patient: 12-hour-old male, full-term, was pink at birth, now blue
Exam: Cyanotic, RR 60, HR 170, SpO2 78% RA → 82% on 100% O2
Pulses: Strong and equal all extremities

What’s your leading diagnosis?

Click for answer **Answer:** Likely Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA) **Why:** - Cyanosis within first day of life - Minimal improvement with O2 (cardiac shunt) - Timing (ductus starting to close) - Strong pulses (not a systemic flow problem) **Action:** - **Immediate transport to pediatric cardiac center** - **Request PGE1** (this baby needs it NOW) - Prepare for intubation (PGE1 causes apnea) - IV access - Keep warm - Continuous monitoring - Contact neonatology/cardiology en route **This baby needs a balloon atrial septostomy and will require arterial switch surgery.**

Case 2: The Fussy Feeder

Patient: 3-week-old female, poor weight gain, sweaty during feeds, fast breathing
Exam: Tachypneic (RR 68), diaphoretic, hepatomegaly, loud holosystolic murmur at LLSB
Vitals: HR 185, SpO2 97% RA
Pulses: Strong

What’s the problem?

Click for answer **Answer:** Congestive Heart Failure from large VSD **Why:** - Classic CHF symptoms in infant: - Diaphoresis during feeds (increased work) - Tachypnea, tachycardia - Poor weight gain (using all calories for breathing/pumping) - Hepatomegaly (fluid backup) - Loud holosystolic murmur at LLSB = VSD - NOT cyanotic (left-to-right shunt, pink baby) **Action:** - **Sit upright** (ease work of breathing) - **Oxygen** (decrease pulmonary vascular resistance) - **IV access** - **Transport to pediatric cardiology** - Consider diuretics if ordered (Lasix) - Minimize stress (keep calm, let parent hold if stable) **This baby will need surgical VSD closure.**

Case 3: The Tet Spell

Patient: 6-month-old male, known Tetralogy of Fallot, awaiting repair
Event: Mom called 911 because baby turned “dark blue” and went limp during diaper change
Current: Deeply cyanotic, lethargic, RR 80, HR 210, SpO2 60%

What do you do?

Click for answer **Answer:** This is a hypercyanotic (Tet) spell - needs immediate intervention **Action:** - **Knee-chest position** (increases SVR → more blood to lungs) - **100% O2** (won't fix shunt but give it anyway) - **IV access** (IO if difficult) - **IV fluid bolus** (10-20 mL/kg NS - increases preload) - **Morphine** 0.1 mg/kg IV (reduces SVR, calms baby) - **Keep calm** (crying worsens spell) - **Consider phenylephrine** if profound hypotension (increases SVR) **Transport to pediatric cardiac center** **If baby arrests:** - CPR - Intubate - Continue knee-chest if possible - Bicarb for acidosis - This is a surgical emergency **Tet spells can be fatal. Aggressive management required.**

Case 4: The Crashing Neonate

Patient: 5-day-old male, born at home, now limp and gray
History: Was fine for first 3 days, then stopped eating, became progressively more lethargic
Exam: Gray, mottled, weak cry, RR 70, HR 220, weak pulses throughout, SpO2 75% on 100% O2
Liver: Palpable 3 cm below costal margin

What’s happening?

Click for answer **Answer:** Duct-dependent systemic lesion (likely HLHS) with ductal closure → cardiogenic shock **Why:** - Timing: 3-7 days of life (ductus closes) - Was fine initially (duct was open) - Rapid deterioration (systemic circulation failing) - Weak pulses (poor systemic perfusion) - Doesn't respond to O2 (cardiac problem) - Hepatomegaly (backward heart failure) **Action:** - **CALL FOR PGE1 IMMEDIATELY** (life-saving) - **IV/IO access** - **Cautious fluid bolus** (5-10 mL/kg max - these babies are in CHF) - **Reduce FiO2 to keep SpO2 75-85%** (counterintuitive but critical) - High O2 → pulmonary vasodilation → blood steals from systemic circulation - **Intubation equipment ready** (PGE1 causes apnea) - **Emergent transport to pediatric cardiac center** - **Inotropic support** if ordered (dopamine, dobutamine) **Without PGE1 and immediate surgical intervention, this baby will die.**

Case 5: The Older Child

Patient: 4-year-old male, squatting after running, moderately cyanotic
History: Known “heart problem,” awaiting surgery
Exam: Blue lips/nailbeds, RR 32, HR 145, SpO2 88% RA
Parent: “He always squats when he’s tired. Doctors say it helps.”

What condition does he likely have?

Click for answer **Answer:** Tetralogy of Fallot (unrepaired) **Why:** - Squatting is pathognomonic for TOF - Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance - This forces more blood through the pulmonary stenosis → more oxygenated blood - Decreases right-to-left shunt - Children learn this instinctively **Action:** - **Allow squatting** (it's therapeutic) - Oxygen - Keep calm - Transport for cardiac evaluation/surgery - If Tet spell develops → manage as above **These kids need surgical repair (complete correction) before school age.**

Reflection

Congenital heart disease is complex, but pattern recognition saves lives.

Here’s what you should know:

✅ Difference between cyanotic and acyanotic lesions
✅ Left-to-right shunts cause CHF (VSD, ASD, PDA)
✅ Right-to-left shunts cause cyanosis (TOF, TGA, truncus)
✅ Duct-dependent lesions need PGE1 to survive
✅ Tet spells require knee-chest + O2 + fluids + morphine
✅ HLHS babies can’t tolerate high O2 (keep SpO2 75-85%)
✅ Timing matters: deterioration at 3-7 days = think closing ductus

Next-level thinking:

  • How do you differentiate respiratory vs. cardiac cyanosis?
  • What’s Eisenmenger syndrome and why does it matter?
  • How do surgical repairs change hemodynamics?
  • What are the long-term complications of CHD repairs?

Your assignment:
Read up on PGE1 protocols in your system. Know where to find it, how to mix it, and when to call for it. One day, you’ll transport a duct-dependent baby—and knowing this cold will save their life.

CHD is scary. But it’s manageable if you understand the physiology.
